summary: The revision answers round 1: it builds on Dependency-Track, sits beside the CRA suites and names SecObserve and CRAVEX. But the new core, Yocto build evidence turned into VEX, is already covered elsewhere: by Yocto's own official sbom-cve-check, by bitvex, by VulnScout and by Lynx Vigiles. The competitor table names none of them. What is left is DT write-back, invalidation and signing, which is thin.

objections.objection: Most dangerous competitor: Bootlin's sbom-cve-check. It has been the Yocto Project's official CVE-monitoring tool since the Wrynose release, it is free (GPLv2), and it works on exactly the inputs VEXpath reads: the SPDX3 SBOM and the vex.bbclass rootfs.json. It marks kernel CVEs not applicable when the affected source file is not compiled in, which is finer than VEXpath's kernel-option rule. It also exports a Yocto VEX manifest with statements and justifications and emits not_affected for disputed CVEs. This is the 'paid additional cut' in the wedge, and every Yocto user now gets it upstream for free.

Lynx (Timesys) Vigiles is an established commercial product for this exact buyer, and the concept leaves it out. Its meta-timesys Yocto layer uploads the kernel and U-Boot .config to filter CVEs and keeps a not-affected list. It markets triage decisions, release-by-release records of how each CVE was handled, VEX export, KEV prioritisation and EU CRA reporting for embedded Linux, Yocto, Buildroot and custom BSPs. It also has NXP as a BSP distribution channel. VEXpath's line that 'nobody affordable turns embedded build evidence into reviewed VEX' is not supported until it is checked against Vigiles' pricing and NXP bundle.

Free open-source tools already cover the rest of the embedded workbench. bitvex is a free CLI that turns Yocto SPDX into OpenVEX using kernel .config, device-tree 'disabled' peripherals and U-Boot config. It also produces delta VEX between builds and has a watch mode that re-scans when SBOMs or configs change, which is close to VEXpath's invalidation idea. VulnScout from Savoir-faire Linux imports Yocto cve-check/VEX with SPDX, has a triage UI, records VEX assessments with AI suggestions that need human approval, and exports CycloneDX and OpenVEX. Device-tree filtering already goes further than VEXpath's MVP.

What remains distinct is two-way Dependency-Track sync, invalidation of inherited decisions and signing with the customer's key. These are workflow features, not a product moat. Any of the above could add them, and so could DT 5.1, since its VEX import already exists. sbom-cve-check output plus DT VEX import already gets most teams the free importer that VEXpath plans to give away.

The EUR 3,480/yr add-on is now priced against free upstream tooling and an incumbent embedded vendor, not only against CRA suites. A buyer adds it on top of a suite at EUR 1,188-3,588, so the triage step costs as much as the whole suite.

strongest_point: I found no tool that keeps per-release VEX decisions natively inside Dependency-Track with conservative invalidation and signing. That gives a narrow but real slot for teams that have standardised on DT.
what_would_change_my_mind: A side-by-side test on 3 real Yocto firmware data sets showing VEXpath resolves 30%+ more findings, with zero wrong not_affected calls, than sbom-cve-check (compiled-sources on) plus bitvex, after both are imported into DT 5.1.
Vigiles pricing or NXP-bundle terms that confirm it is out of reach or a poor fit for 50-500-person makers, plus 3 discovery calls where Vigiles or VulnScout users name a gap VEXpath fills.

A repositioning onto the free upstream tools rather than against them, for example a supported, DT-native ledger and signing layer on sbom-cve-check output, sold with Bootlin, Savoir-faire Linux or a Yocto consultancy as a signed partner.
Evidence that DT maintainers will not take Yocto VEX import and cross-release decision inheritance into scope within 12 months.

resolved_prior.objection: Dependency-Track 5.1 and funded CSAF work close the gap (most dangerous competitor in round 1).
resolved_prior.note: Repositioned to build on DT: it writes back into DT's analysis and consumes DT's CSAF when that lands. This conflict is gone, but DT plus free Yocto tooling still sets the free baseline.

resolved_prior.objection: Missed self-serve CRA suites (CVD Portal, CRA Evidence, CRA-Ready) priced below VEXpath.
resolved_prior.note: The suites are now listed, the Art. 14 workflow and evidence pack are dropped, and VEXpath is sold beside them. The add-on still costs as much as a whole suite.

resolved_prior.objection: Free SecObserve and DejaCode/CRAVEX cover the VEX workbench.
resolved_prior.note: Both are named and the product is differentiated on embedded build evidence. That differentiation now collides with sbom-cve-check, bitvex and VulnScout.

resolved_prior.objection: sbomify is a closer rival than a partner.
resolved_prior.note: The hosted portal is dropped, sbomify is framed as an integration target and a possible rival, and the risk is kept.

resolved_prior.objection: Funded enterprise vendors could add a self-serve tier within a quarter.
resolved_prior.note: Unchanged by design. An embedded-specialist incumbent, Lynx Vigiles, already covers the Yocto build-evidence segment and is missing from the analysis.

resolved_prior.objection: The defensible core (CSAF matching) is a perishable feature, not a product.
resolved_prior.note: The core moved to build-evidence rules, and those are already free upstream (sbom-cve-check compiled-source filtering, bitvex kernel/DT/U-Boot filters) and commercial (Vigiles kernel config filter). The feature-not-product problem remains.
